quotedTweet.text:
🚨 Happening now. The High Court is delivering judgment in a landmark standoff between the judges of the Supreme Court of Kenya and the body that can recommend their removal from office.

The background. Every judge of the Supreme Court went to the High Court to challenge whether the Judicial Service Commission, the body that handles complaints against judges, can entertain complaints that are really an attack on the merits of their judgments. In plain terms, the judges say a party who loses a case should not be able to turn the complaints process into a second appeal against a decision they did not like.

The matter is before a three judge bench of Justices Kariuki, Mugambi and Mwamuye.
A caveat first. The judgment is still being read from the bench as we write. What follows is the court's reasoning so far, and it is not final until the court concludes.
The determination so far. The decision appears to be unanimous, and the court framed seven issues for determination. 
Three already stand out.

✅ First, on the court's own power to hear the case. Under Article 165 of the Constitution, the High Court holds supervisory jurisdiction. The independence given to the Commission is not the same as immunity. Its actions, and its failures to act, can be examined in court, because no public body sits above the Constitution, and the court may inquire whether what the Commission did was constitutional.

✅ Second, on what the Commission must do before calling a judge to answer. The court held that the Commission is not a mere postbox that receives a complaint and forwards it on. It must carry out an initial threshold assessment and filter out complaints that are frivolous.

✅ Third, on running two processes at once. Where a complainant takes the same grievance to the High Court and to the Commission at the same time, there is no blanket rule, but the court must look at the real substance of both. Where they genuinely overlap, pursuing both can amount to an abuse of the court process.

On one side is the independence of the Judiciary. A judge must be free to decide a case without fear that the losing party will retaliate with a removal complaint. On the other is accountability. The Commission has a constitutional duty to receive genuine complaints about how judges conduct themselves, and that duty should not be hollowed out. The hard line is between a true complaint about how a judge behaved and a disguised appeal against what a judge decided.

✅ Four further issues remain to be read, and the final orders will show how far the court has gone.

👉 Follow @Lexken_EMSLaw for practical legal insights on constitutional law and the Judiciary.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

The disturbing AI deepfake incident that has rightly angered our industry should not be looked at as an isolated incident.

It is a warning.

Ram Pothineni made an important point: “They’re faceless, so they’re fearless.” His suggestion of Aadhaar-linked accountability for online identities deserves serious discussion. Freedom of expression must always be protected. But anonymity cannot become a weapon to abuse, defame, sexually violate or deliberately destroy someone.

And this problem does not begin or end with deepfakes.

For quite some time, I have been concerned about organised and targeted negativity against films, actors and filmmakers within our own industry.

A film should succeed or fail because audiences watch it and decide. Criticism, reviews, trolling and disagreement are part of cinema today.

But a coordinated campaign to damage a film before audiences have even seen it is not criticism. It is sabotage.

Sundeep Kishan recently spoke publicly about targeted, paid negativity against him and his film even before its release. The Paradise had to approach a court before release seeking protection against defamatory and damaging content. These are not issues we should casually dismiss.

Behind every film are years of work, hundreds of families and producers risking enormous amounts of money.

Watch the film. Love it. Hate it. Criticise it brutally if you genuinely feel that way.

But first, LET THE FILM RELEASE.

What is even more unfortunate is that some of this comes from within our own ecosystem: fan groups fighting fan groups, anonymous pages pretending to be neutral, and accounts using photographs of actors as their DPs while behaving in ways those actors may never endorse.

THE VIBE MANUFACTURING PLAYBOOK

1. Measure everything. Digital calipers for small parts, a phone LiDAR app like Polycam to scan a space or an object. Bad measurements are the #1 reason first builds fail

2. Have a frontier model write the design as code. Describe the part to a model like Claude Opus 5.5 or Astra, and have it write the design in a codebased CAD tool like OpenSCAD or CadQuery. Zoo's Text to CAD does it in one step!

3. Use real CAD files. The text to 3D models on Hugging Face make shapes that look right, but factories need precise files: STEP for machined parts, DXF for lasercut metal, STL for 3D printing

4. Make sure it can be made. Ask the AI to check the design against how factories actually work: how tight metal can bend, how small a hole can be, how much wiggle room parts need etc...

5. Prototype in plastic first. A $300 to $600 home 3D printer like a Bambu Lab lets you test the fit overnight before paying for metal (really fun to play with too!)

6. Pay an engineer for 1 hour. Before your first real order, have a mechanical engineer on Upwork etc review the files. It's the cheapest insurance you'll ever buy.

7. Send it out. SendCutSend cuts and bends metal, Xometry and Protolabs handle machining and plastic, JLCPCB builds circuit boards. Instant quotes, and parts usually ship in days.

8. Add the brains. Most smart features run on a cheap wifi chip like the ESP32. Design the board in KiCad, and use ESPHome to control it straight from your phone.

9. Make one, then fix it. Your first version will be off somewhere! Order a single unit, test it, and adjust.

10. Do the math. Add up parts, finishing, assembly, packaging, and shipping. Custom products are hard to resell, so price for healthy margins.

11. Sell the design and make to order. Let customers adjust the measurements, and only manufacture after they pay. Zero warehouse, zero unsold stock.

12. Handle the boring part. If it plugs into a wall or touches kids, you'll need safety certification. It's slow and annoying, which is exactly why it's a moat.

13. Scale when it works. Once orders are steady, switch to batch runs and your cost per unit drops fast.

text:
Why some countries have banned starlink in India?

Countries ban or restrict Starlink for five primary reasons

• Local Market Protection: Domestic internet providers frequently lobby regulators to block Starlink to prevent it from undercutting local businesses with predatory pricing.

• Loss of State Control: Governments cannot easily monitor, filter, or intercept satellite traffic, stripping them of data oversight and censorship capabilities.

• National Security Risks: Broadly accessible, unmonitored networks raise fears of foreign espionage, unauthorized military use, or illegal communication channels.

• Ownership Laws: Many nations require foreign telecom companies to have local equity or citizens owning a specific percentage of shares (e.g., South Africa and Namibia).

• Regulatory Non-Compliance: Starlink often ships hardware or activates services in territories before securing formal regulatory licenses and spectrum approvals.

text:
Global Access Map: Where Starlink is Blocked or Awaiting Approval
While SpaceX’s Starlink now operates in over 100 countries, significant global coverage gaps remain due to geopolitical sanctions, state security policies, and pending spectrum licenses.
1. Restricted & State-Banned Nations
(Blocked due to state monopolies, security restrictions, or international sanctions)
 * China: Banned to protect domestic space and satellite constellations (Guowang / Qianfan).
 * Russia: Banned due to national security concerns and military restrictions.
 * Iran: Blocked locally under strict state internet control and US sanctions.
 * North Korea: Total state-enforced telecommunications blackout.
 * Syria: Under comprehensive international sanctions and state regulatory blocks.
 * Cuba: Restricted under US embargo provisions and state telecommunications law.
 * Belarus: Blocked under regional security arrangements and active sanctions.
 * Afghanistan: Unapproved under current administrative and telecommunications rules.
 * Myanmar: Banned by the military regime, with strict prohibitions on satellite hardware.
 * Venezuela: Lacks operational authorization and regulatory agreements.
2. Pending Regulatory & Spectrum Approvals
(Applications submitted or trials underway, awaiting final commercial clearance)
 * India: Awaiting finalized administrative spectrum allocations, pricing, and national security clearances.
 * South Africa: Held up by the mandatory 30% local equity ownership rule for telecom operators.
 * Pakistan: Pending technical and security evaluation by the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA).
 * Vietnam: Subject to mandatory local data storage and joint-venture corporate requirements.
 * Thailand: Under review by the NBTC regarding foreign satellite licensing guidelines.
 * Turkey: Pending national spectrum assignment and BTK regulatory approval.
 * Saudi Arabia: Ongoing discussions covering CITC licensing and localized infrastructure.
 * UAE: Commercial satellite broadband applications currently under review by TDRA.
 * Bangladesh: Technical trials completed; awaiting final spectrum license terms.
 * Egypt: Subject to military and national telecom regulatory agency approvals.
3. Regulatory Crackdowns on Grey-Market Imports
In several markets without direct licenses (notably Zimbabwe, Cameroon, Sudan, and Namibia), local telecom authorities have penalized the illicit importation of roaming terminals, prompting SpaceX to enforce geofencing until commercial licenses are granted.

SDGs Conference 2026 - Panel Session 3: Press Freedom and Independent Journalism as a Cross-Cutting Enabler of PeacePanel examined how independent journalism, press freedom, media literacy, and journalist safety contribute to peace and public trust. Moderator Joyce Davis, Opinion Editor, PennLive, opened by noting that journalism depends on asking difficult questions and telling important stories—and that communities are less able to make informed decisions when those questions cannot be asked safely. 
 🎤 Journalist and Co-Founder of Peek TV, based in India, Priyanshi Sharma discussed the increasingly blurred line between journalists, influencers, and activists on social media. She described how independent reporters can bring attention to stories ignored by mainstream outlets, citing coverage of a major protest in India that she said was largely absent from television news.
 🎤Nigerian journalist Femi Adesina warned that AI-generated falsehoods and fabricated stories can erode confidence in media institutions. He urged journalists to follow professional ethics, verify information repeatedly, and avoid publishing claims they cannot substantiate.  
🎤Australian Journalist Karen Percy highlighted threats facing women journalists, including online abuse, sexualized harassment, physical violence, and unequal treatment in newsrooms. These pressures can silence reporters and limit whose experiences are represented. 
 🎤 Abdülhamit Bilici, Journalist and Media Executive connected press freedom to quality of life, arguing that independent reporting can expose corruption and hold power accountable. Drawing on his experience after his Turkish newspaper, Zaman, was seized and shut down, he stressed that journalists cannot defend press freedom alone; broader public and institutional support is essential.

Hey everyone and @SamsungIndia Story start from 23 April 2026 till today, I have been trapped in what feels like a complete service scam by Samsung’s authorized service centre in Dharampeth, Nagpur, Maharashtra.

I discovered a sudden issue in the 0.6x ultra-wide camera of my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The phone was never dropped, never mishandled. After researching online, I found MANY users reporting the exact same issue with the new 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Reddit, YouTube, Samsung Community — same problem everywhere.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

I informed the service centre on WhatsApp. They ignored the messages.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

And suddenly their excuse became:
“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

Imagine buying one of Samsung’s most powerful flagship phones and being told GAMING can void service support.

When I asked for a written denial letter, they REFUSED.

When I started recording for proof, they stopped answering questions and began ignoring me completely.

I had no option left except calling the police.

ONLY after police intervention did the entire attitude of the service centre change. Suddenly:
“We never denied service.”
“We are ready to repair.”

They even requested police officers to convince me to delete the videos I recorded.

After another repair attempt, they told me:
“Do not use BGMI for 12 hours.”

I followed everything they said.

Result?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Since then I have been continuously emailing Samsung support and Kajal from customer experience, asking for a permanent solution or replacement because I cannot travel 13KM repeatedly for the SAME ISSUE.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Absolutely shameful. @SamsungMobile @SamsungIndia

text:
We have dealt with solicitors who told us not to contact their client, the landlord. We have not contacted him, but he keeps texting us. When we reply, he then texts back telling us to stop texting him. We need to raise this with the lawyers: who is supposed to be dealing with what.

We have received this letter. Kimberley signed for it at the door. It is addressed to Miss Kimberley Bath, McDonnell Court. It should have been addressed to me. It has “mental health” marked at the top. I do not think that is fair.

Look at the paperwork. See how it has been ripped open? It has already been opened. It was not sealed properly. We have the same interference with the mail again. It has a Ledingham Chalmers solicitors stamp on the back, and a mental health postal stamp. We will see what they say. I predict they will say they spoke to their client, he accepts responsibility for the doors and windows, and he will get them fixed. There will be nothing about the heating, and nothing about the claim. We asked for £5,000. If anything has come back on that, it will be a rejection.

Working out what we would be entitled to for the length of time we have been here, if we go to the Housing and Property Chamber, the figure is about £35,000. We have only asked for £5,000. We will see what the lawyer has said.

The letter says they are writing on behalf of their clients, Gary and Alison Smith, the landlords of the property in which we currently reside at 78B Duke Street, Aberdeen, AB24 3HB. It is a response to an email received on Tuesday 16 April 2024 with a link to a video recording. They say they have listened to the entire recording, discussed it with their client, and been instructed to address a number of points.

They say that throughout the video we claimed both clients were not registered landlords, and that Gary in particular was acting as an agent. They say that is incorrect, and that both are registered landlords with Aberdeen Council, with registration numbers that can be checked on the council website.

That registration is recent. When we first took the tenancy, Alison Smith was registered and Gary was doing all the talking. He provided the keys and came back to see the property a couple of times in the first year. It was him who later abandoned the property. Alison Smith was abusive about the property, which caused me to call the police. Gary turned up boisterous until he realised we were on the phone to the police. That video will be at the end of this recording.

They may be registered now, but they have not been registered for the whole tenancy. We have screenshots of the registration for this house showing periods when it was deregistered and not in anyone’s name. It has now been re-registered in Gary Smith and Alison Smith’s names. We need the date of that registration. We also have video of Kimberley at the council, where it was confirmed that neither Gary nor Alison was registered at that time. We have that in letter form and on audio. We can defeat any claim at the Housing and Property Chamber that Gary and Alison Smith were the registered landlords of this property continuously from 20 September 2020.

The letter says we raised several issues about the condition of the property, that we told Gary, and that he did not fix them. Their clients say only two issues were brought to their attention. One was a broken shower around 12 to 18 months ago. Gary says that when he heard about it he arranged for a plumber to fix it, and that he can produce the invoice. I agree he did fix it, but only after we reported that we had no shower and went without one for about six months. My body temperature drops and I need to get into hot water. We have three days of video of me severely ill, vomiting, drinking milk to cool the acid and vomiting it straight back up. These episodes come on when I cannot get a hot shower or bath. There is a name for the condition. I cannot pronounce it and I cannot remember it. Being at an address with no hot water is dangerous for me.

I believe the shower was reported about 40 months ago. I have a recorded telephone call telling Gary the shower was broken. He did nothing for several months. Only when Kimberley persevered on one particular day, explaining my health and that I needed a shower, did he visit. He was not pleasant. He said things to Kimberley that are open to question, including that the only reason he allowed her to live here was because he knew what she was going through. That is the same pattern we have seen with landlords and letting agents in the north-east of Scotland. The letter misstates the priority given to the shower, the need for hot water, and my health.

When it was fitted, the joiner told me to wait until morning for the sealant. I still got in that shower, kept water off the unit, and sat there for hours. I still have to do that.

He fixed the shower only after a long period without one, and during a period when no one was registered for the property.

They say the only other issue raised directly with Gary, when he was at the property, was the kitchen roof. They say my carer, Mr James Fraser, brought it to his attention, that Gary undertook to arrange a repair, but that Mr Fraser insisted he would repair it himself because it was minor, and that no further damage has been reported. They say they cannot be held responsible for any other alleged issues if they were not reported and they had no knowledge of them.

That is not right. We have every recorded telephone call and text to Gary and Alison Smith, where Gary was the person who responded. We reported the doors, windows, shower and toilet. We have video of Gary at the address every time he visited, just as we have video of the joiner who visited today. Every word is recorded. Gary knows about the toilet, the shower and the sinks. We have him on video looking at the sink and saying he would go to B&Q or another hardware store for the proper taps. As it stands, the sink has been running for almost two years. If you try to turn the taps off, the pipes buzz. We think that is pressure from other tenants in the building. We have it set so it does not buzz, but when someone else uses water it starts again, so it tends to run all the time. Water leaks down the pipes. The back of the kitchen is mouldy. Gary has been told. The condition today is the result of his failure to get it fixed at the time. His solicitors have been misinformed. He may be busy and may not remember everything. When they see the videos of him in the house, he may remember.

On the ceiling, it was discussed on camera. I said I would fix it. But after flood after flood, the damage is more extensive. It is structural, not cosmetic. The wall that holds the ceiling is splitting. One part of the wall in the corner is straight by a spirit level, but where the big crack is, the wall is leaning into the kitchen, which is parting the ceiling in the middle of the living room. That cannot be fixed with plasterboard. I think I pointed this out to Gary when he came back to look at the toilet, the kitchen sink and other parts. He was aware of the ceiling, and I told him I thought it was structural. At the time both he and I thought it was cosmetic and easy to fix. It is not. The wall is moving and parting the living-room ceiling. Where the letter says I insisted I would repair it myself because it was minor, and that they had no knowledge of other issues, we disagree. We will add the other videos of Gary at this address, showing issues reported over a long period, until he told us not to contact him and abandoned the property and the problems he had witnessed. He is on video saying he would go to a hardware store, I am sure he mentioned B&Q, for parts for the toilet, which constantly runs, and the sink, which constantly runs. He looked at the extractor fan in the toilet, saw it did not work, and said it needed replacing. There was also the front door. The original door was broken by the police and by Orbis joiners. It would not fit back into the latch. Gary gave me permission to change the fascia so the latch would fit. That was not possible, because the door I got had to go into its own frame. That is the door there today.

My memory of dates over four years may be foggy. Anyone’s would be. The recordings are time-stamped and dated, and can be checked against the property. We can show that their clients have misled them.

The main reason they can be held responsible is that the house is below the tolerable standard for many reasons. There is no proper fire protection. The property is not fit for the letting market. As registered landlords, the council had a duty to inspect and check that what the registration purported was actually being provided. It has not been. I find it astounding that they deny knowledge of particular issues when I have it on video.

They say that on entry the property was in good tenantable repair, with no mould or damp, and that any mould and damp now is likely from lack of ventilation or the way the property is used. So we are to blame. They say it has not been reported. They say all appliances and fixtures were in good order at the start and the property was fit to let, and that any claim is misconceived.

It is not misconceived. We have strong points on harassment and denial of access to services. Gary was at the address, on camera, seeing the faulty sink and saying he would fix it. If he has not fixed it for two years, mould and damp follow. That is not about how we use the property. We have had to boil and drink from the hot tap because it cannot be turned off. With the mixer, cold comes through mixed with hot from another line. That water is not treated as drinking water. We cannot get proper drinking water at this address. It has affected us, including gut problems. Phil is drinking tea. Gary’s claim that he had no knowledge is false. He was in the house, witnessing the faults, and saying he would get them fixed.

The letter then refers to an undisputed lack of rental payments for the four years the lease was in operation, and says their clients are likely to succeed in a claim for arrears at the First-tier Tribunal. It says failure to obtain housing benefit is not a defence, because it is not the landlord’s job to apply for a tenant’s benefits, although they understand Gary tried to assist.

He did attend the council with Kimberley and asked why he was not getting his rent. The reason rent is not being paid, even if it were available from the council, is the tolerable standard. When Gary recognised the property was not above the tolerable standard, he should have offered a rent reduction immediately. He did not. He kept trying to charge the same rent. If he applies to the Housing and Property Chamber for arrears, we will attend with years of video and audio showing the state of the property, how long we have been deprived of services, the effect on our lives, and the lack of heating. He is not entitled to that rent in the first place.

Gary entered an agreement under which Kimberley was renting the property, including an additional room for overnight stay by a carer. There is a European and domestic line of authority on housing policy, rent arrears and rent relief not being applied properly in favour of pushing disabled people onto Universal Credit. In Scotland the approach has been to put disabled people on Universal Credit and then pay the rent. We say Aberdeen City Council’s conduct has included hate-related treatment, recorded on video, and that they tried to move Kimberley onto Universal Credit before the disability elements were in place. She has been evicted from three addresses because of what we say are ultra vires decisions, contrary to the Scotland Act 1998. That is why council rent has not been paid into Kimberley’s account. Even if it had been, she would have held it until the tolerable standard was met. If the landlord abandoned repairs, she is entitled to instruct a qualified tradesman and apply that month’s rent, and the next month’s if the cost exceeds the £550 that should have been paid.

There is no realistic prospect of Gary succeeding at the Housing and Property Chamber on the evidence we have. When we moved in, we recognised a pattern we had seen with previous landlords and letting agents. I am asking the police to investigate what I believe is organised interference: denial of heating, hot water and cooking facilities, year after year, across many addresses over more than ten years — 23 addresses in 16 years. Some of those landlords and agents later told us that Aberdeen City Council was hostile to us, and that information about me came first from the police and then from the council, which led landlords to treat us abusively: threats, attempts to remove Kimberley from the door while she was having a panic attack, and police turning a blind eye. I want the criminal side of Gary and Alison Smith’s behaviour on a particular date looked at, and the same pattern from landlord to landlord.

The letter says everything worked when the property was let. It might be lawful for an owner-occupier. To put it on the letting market they needed to think about fire doors and the rest of the standards. A joiner did attend today. We allowed access. He was polite. He measured the windows and the door. He measured the door in the wrong place. I pointed out that the original frame is still there, so the new door has to fit from that point. He remeasured and thanked me. He would not have known that, because he had not fitted a door there before and I had. We agreed he would go away and see what he could do. He did not say when he would be back. We have no proper lock security on the door. The solicitors’ advice that the landlord should not speak to us has assisted the abandonment of the property. The shower was fitted one day after about four or five months of calls, and we had largely given up until I was seriously ill. We are used to cold water at many addresses: Boddam in 2018 to 2019, Froghall Terrace from 2019 to 2020, and here from 2020 to date.

We also have recordings of people who were asked to act against us and later spoke more honestly once they saw the effect on Kimberley’s health, including a stroke, and the condition she has been living in. Gary had a duty to assist in preventing antisocial behaviour and to involve the council. The police had a duty too. Gary’s friends have been at this address. One had a key. We have recorded mail being taken and reported it. Police have attended. Credit cards, driving licences, gold rings and stolen mail have been left at the address.

One morning I caught an elderly resident taking everybody’s mail from the communal mailbox, on CCTV. The recording is still on the drive, time-stamped, and bagged with a list of what is on it. Every visit by Gary, and every time he was told about a defect, is on a drive and on other recordings. After she took the mail and shut the box, I went to the door as she left. We often leave the front door open in the morning to air the house, as my mother did, regardless of temperature. The door is open as I speak. I videoed her putting the mail into another container. I kept the camera on it, opened it, and with gloves bagged and sealed everyone’s envelopes, with notes of how it happened. I have put the relevant footage together showing theft, damage, harassment and the same neighbour behaviour we have seen at other addresses after police have spoken to people. Gary is not outside that pattern.

Other landlords have succeeded at the Housing and Property Chamber because legal points sent to the legal chair were never answered. Before a proof, the chair said no legal points had been entered. We have a year and a half of video, audio and recorded calls of clerks not understanding why points were not being answered, and months of clerks emailing, every time we phoned, asking us to correct the spelling and send it back.

On rent, there are cases where a landlord knew of a failed service or appliance, did not fix it promptly, and did not offer a rent reduction. It is the failure to offer the reduction that holds the landlord to account, and the sheriff has treated that as meaning the landlord is not entitled to the full rent. I have that authority and will use it on any Housing and Property Chamber application. We have already lodged a failure-to-repair application and set it out in detail. We have the same problem with email attachments not opening. I am surprised these solicitors could open the link and watch the video, because the Crown, the sheriff court, the tribunal service, Aberdeen City Council, the Sheriff Appeal Court and the High Court have all said they cannot open our attachments. The First-tier Tribunal has said the same in this case. That interference protects Gary.

Modus operandi rattled again.

text:
Two Muslim women journalists on Thursday alleged that they were beaten by Delhi police personnel in South Delhi’s Saket police station. The two journalists said that a police team detained them and took them to the Saket police station, where they were assaulted.The journalists were on assignment to cover an event attended by Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, following which the assault occurred, the journalists alleged. 

The journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafessa Khan alleged that they were dragged by their hair upstairs and were met with brutish assault for approximately 40 mins. 

“They dragged us upstairs by our hair and brutally assaulted us there. When they became exhausted from beating us, they stopped to take a break.”  Journalist Shaheen Khan told FoEJ Media. 

Both the journalists further claimed that on learning about their Muslim identity, the assault was intensified. 

“When they found out that we were Muslims, she said, ‘You’re Muslim? Now I’ll beat you even more'” Shaheen said. 

“She told me, ‘You’re Muslim? I’ll hit you three or four more times.’ She then struck me so hard with a lathi that the injury is still swollen.”  Nafeesa added, showing her bruises to FoEJ Media. 

Revealing the start of the assault, Shaheen said, “I was standing downstairs, speaking to my family over the phone and informing them about what had happened. Meanwhile, a female police officer approached me and demanded that I hand over my phone. When I told her, ‘Please tell me what happened; whatever you need to discuss, we can discuss it here,’ she replied, ‘I have a different way of talking. We’ll talk upstairs.’” 

“Listen to the language she used. She said, ‘I have a different way of talking. I’ll speak to you upstairs.'” Shaheen highlighted.

“She snatched my phone and started slapping me,” she added. 

Both the journalists further alleged that they were refused to have water even when they were falling to grasp the air due to the continuous assault. 

“When we asked, ‘Ma’am, please give us some water,’ she replied, ‘We will beat you thirsty,'” Shaheen alleged.

“Nafeesa’s condition deteriorated, and she collapsed unconscious. I told them that she needed medical attention, but no one paid any heed,” she added. 

The incident occurred on Thursday morning when the Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta attended the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket. 

The journalist said that they had gone to cover the event; however, they were stopped by police and taken to Saket police station, where the assault was launched. 

In an official statement, DCP (South) Anant Mittal described the allegations as “factually incorrect and misleading.”

“Claims suggesting otherwise, including allegations of assault for asking questions to the Hon’ble Chief Minister, are totally false, misleading, and baseless. Citizens and social media users are advised to refrain from circulating unverified and misleading information,” read the statement.  

The police said that despite multiple requests and instructions to remove the vehicles and clear the route, they refused to remove them. Following the security and safety protocol of the VVIP route, both the journalists were taken to the local police station for the inquiry, the police said, and the Hindustan Times highlighted. 

“In recent days, 4pm has been consistently raising serious questions and publishing reports on matters related to the Delhi government and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta. In such a context, it is natural to wonder whether today’s action is connected to those reports and questions in any way.” said Sanjay Sharma, the editor-in-chief of 4pm News Network. 

“Since when has asking questions of the Chief Minister become a crime? Since when has a journalist’s question become so dangerous for those in power? And can a journalist having ‘Khan’ in their name become a reason for assaulting them?” he posted on X. 

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

The incident was also condemned by the political leaders. Congress posted the video on X, while members of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) have condemned the alleged use of force against journalists and accused the government of failing to protect press freedom. Indian Youth Congress leader Darshan Kaushik speaking to FoEJ Media said, “It is extremely shameful that two girls were subjected to brutality after being asked about their religion. In such a context, it is natural to wonder whether today’s action is connected to those reports and questions in any way.” said Sanjay Sharma, the editor-in-chief of 4pm News Network. 

“Since when has asking questions of the Chief Minister become a crime? Since when has a journalist’s question become so dangerous for those in power? And can a journalist having ‘Khan’ in their name become a reason for assaulting them?” he posted on X. 

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

text:
Last week I saved a man’s life. He’s 77 years old and a good close friend of mine. He was declining after he lost the charging device to his insulin pump. I saw it coming a week ahead of time and asked him what I was supposed to do if he fell and didn’t have his phone. He didn’t have an answer. He had fallen in his garage. He had fallen by his pool. I called every morning to make sure he was ok. 

One morning I called and he didn’t answer. Then I called later that day and it went straight to voicemail which told me his phone didn’t get charged. I decided if I couldn’t get ahold of him the next morning I would call the police. Fortunately that next morning, he answered. 

A few days later however, he answered my morning call from his kitchen floor. He had been there since the day before. Why he didn’t call someone would become apparent later. He told me, if I can just get some fluids I’ll be ok. I told him I would have Jenny call for help. He disconnected the call. Jenny called the police and they sent the paramedics and he went to the hospital. 

He had emergency surgery to remove his inflamed gallbladder then was in the ICU for a few days. He has since been move to a physical therapy facility to be rehabilitated. 

He once told me, “when I die, you’ll be a very wealthy man”

When it came down to it, I saved his life. 

I guess that makes me too good for my own intelligence. 

I’ve never needed the money more than I do now. 😒

ICYMI: The Day the Director of Forensic Services in Police Was Ordered by a Judge to Answer Questions as Asked and Not as he Wants Them Asked. 

This was 2 years ago in the still ongoing trial of Uganda Vs MollyKatanga and 4 others. 

Mr Andrew K. Mubiru had just finished giving DNA forensic evidence on behalf of the state.

He had told court that he had analyzed and reported DNA evidence in the trial.

Time for cross examination came and the defense put it on the record that the state had denied them most of the documents pertaining to the tests Mr Mubiru had conducted; same tests the state wanted to rely on to secure convictions against their clients.

The state on their part said they weren’t under duty to disclose laboratory protocols, procedures or any such background information. But they had disclosed the final DNA report. The methods used to get it be damned or they were a national security issue.

But they offered their witness to be cross examined on that.

Defense Attorney @elisonk took the first stab at it.

Judge Isaac Muwata to Mr Elison Karuhanga: You can proceed with cross examination 
EK: Much obliged my Lord. For the record, Elison Karuhanga….

Mr Mubiru, you prepared a report for purposes of this hearing, correct? Yes?
AM: That’s true, my Lord
EK: You’ll agree with me that this report contains all the tests you carried out on the exhibits in this case?
AM: My Lord all the tests that we conduct, the outcomes and findings, we detail them in a report that is submitted to court.
Judge: No, you refer to this report, not to others
AM: This report, my Lord 
EK: My Lord, let me ask the question again. 
Mr Mubiru, you’ll agree that this report contains all the tests you carried out on the exhibits that you received. 
AM: My Lord the tests conducted on the exhibits I received are detailed in the report that is submitted to court.
EK: You’ll also agree that the report contains all the exhibits you received in this case?
AM: My Lord, the exhibits I received are detailed in the report that is submitted to court
EK: I think if you just help us quicken the answers with yes or no where yes or no can do…
AM: My Lord the exhibits that I received and examined are detailed in the report that is submitted to court
EK: So, that’s a yes? And this report contains all the tests you carried out on those exhibits?
AM: For every exhibit, I carried out a test which is detailed in the report; and the findings thereof. 
EK: So, Mr Mubiru, it would be fair to say that this report is conclusive and you have nothing to add, subtract or remove?
AM: My Lord, the report is as per the findings, with my inferences and opinions therein. 
EK: Is this report conclusive and do you have anything to add or not?
Judge Muwata to Mr Mubiru: You refer to the question you’ve been asked, not which one you decide. 
AM: My Lord, the report has findings on the tests that I conducted 
EK insists: is it conclusive?
AM still tries to skirt the question: the tests are conclusive 
EK digs in some more: so, is this a conclusive report?
AM: The report is to the end that I have an opinion based on the data I have. 
Judge: the report is….
AM: the report contains….EK cuts him off: the report is conclusive?
AM: the report contains my opinion based on the data
EK: is there anything you have to add or subtract from your report?
AM: My Lord, the report has an opinion 
EK: do you have anything to add or subtract from the report? (Yes/No). Please answer what you’re being asked
AM: My Lord, my opinion is in the report
EK wasn’t letting him get away with it. He asked again: so, do you have anything to add or subtract? 
AM: it depends. If the circumstances change, I can change my opinion 
EK: Okay, so you’re not bound by this report?
AM: I’m bound by the report as per the circumstances under which I examined the exhibits. 

This tap dance set the tone with which an, at times, bare knuckles cross examination that spread across two months was conducted. 

Video: @BbegMedia

text:
“When I was pregnant with you I was under pressure to have an abortion but I refused. I chose instead to bring you into this world.” 

Excerpts from "Magoba Ga Uganda" the Auto Biography of Pastor Martin Ssempa..now Coming out later in Dec 2025. Give me some feedback. 

My mother did not hesitate to bring up the circumstances around my birth and conception every time I tried her patience as a young boy. Granted, she always told me she loved me, but I got to know my chequered history quite early. “Your father’s parents owned a shop and the women who worked there assured me that it was unacceptable and totally reprehensible, a taboo, for an African woman and an Asian man to get together, let alone produce a child from that union. The only solution they said, was to perform an abortion and end that life before it even began. But I refused!" 

I was conceived towards the end of the 60s, a few years into Uganda’s journey as an independent country, a few years before Idi Amin Dada started his rule in Uganda. I am told it was the time of miniskirts and twist dancing in Uganda, and the time of the American sex revolution! My father was a young Asian of (most likely) Indian descent whose family was one of the trading families in Masaka. 

He was a student at Makerere University, and that is the extent of my knowledge about my father. Soon after I was born, President Iddi Amin declared an economic war of indigenization and my father was among those who were deported/expelled out of Uganda. The History of Uganda is such that Asians, particularly Indians took the lion’s share of trading licences. President Amin wanted to reverse this unfair advantage but unfortunately, it meant I would never get to meet my father or his family. Not only was I born in a conflicted relationship of races, I never got a chance to know who my father was, nor his family. Despite the great love and acceptance that I received from my mother, siblings and my Baganda tribal family, I always felt a great sense of “father hunger” - that yearning for fatherly protection, provision and affirmation which only a Dad could provide. 

My mother was a primary school teacher who was struggling to raise eight children as a single parent. She had been married to James Kyeyune, a medical officer and they were blessed with six children but their marriage broke down. My mother always told me that she could not accept being a co-wife. My step father had brought another wife home and she could not accept the idea of sharing a husband. Despite the efforts of the good catholic bishops who intervened to smooth things over, the marriage broke down and she moved away in the mid-60s to start a new life as a teacher and a single mother. I was born into a family of seven other children, five boys and two girls. Dickson, the eldest had gone off to join the police force, Joseph the second born and Edward the fifth born stayed with their paternal grandparents. Clare and Fred were students in a Catholic boarding school and came home only during the holidays. This meant that the three youngest children Florence, John and myself were the ones who stayed home with mother. 

Owing to my bi-racial parentage, my looks were quite different from the rest of the family and the children around me. I had big curly hair unlike my brother’s kinky hair. I had much lighter skin due to my father’s suspected Asian descent. In our Baganda culture, the name of a child is based on the clan of the father and in the absence of my biological father, my mother gave me the names of her father, Ssempa which meant that I belonged to my mother’s clan; symbolically represented by the colobus monkey (Nkima). My grandfather, Alipo Ssempa was an educated British colonial government administrator and interpreter in Masaka. Sadly, I never got to meet him as death took him before we could meet. His father, Bisakka or Bishaka who was my great grandfather had been a noteworthy regional trader in the Buganda, Ankole, Bunyoro, Rwanda and Tanzania region. 

He was called Bisaka, a name very closely related to Kisaka which is a large cluster or collection of trees and bushes which occurs on the savannah plains and hills in this region. It’s like an individual collection of a family of trees and bushes which are separated from others by savannah grass fields. Just as his name implies, my great grandfather had eighty wives which made up his large family! Bisaka was known as Bishaka by the western Ankole-Rwanda tribes whose language is characterized by the ‘sh’ making him multi tribal/multi lingual and multi-wifey. Unfortunately, this great trader and lover of the sweet affections of the beautiful women of Buganda, Ankole, Rwanda and Tanzania region suffered an early death which led to the scattering of the whole family. 

My great grandmother "Venecka Munaku Atambuza Mwoyo" [the poor walks guided by the spirit] and her sister who had also been a co-wife branched out Eastward and settled between Mityebiri/ Minziro in Rakai and Buyikuzi in Lukaya which is half way between Kampala city and Masaka town. Thus I carried the genes of Bisaka and the name of his son Ssempa, a fact which made people do a double take every time they met the bi-racial child with a native African name. It was not the norm. 

These bio-genetical differences were much more pronounced in my childhood. I stuck out both in the classroom and on the children’s playfield. I can compare it to being the only black student in an all-white students school or being the only white student at an all-black-African students school. To some, I was an object of curiosity and I often had to bear the discomfort of having my hair felt, so the kids with kinky hair could feel my curly hair. Most of them were kind, but others would mock me with unkind words, ”Ssempa was forgotten at the airport, the Indians forgot him with the suitcases and boxes at the airport.” They would laugh and others gave me the monicker, ‘Magoba ga Uganda’ a Luganda phrase meaning “Ugandan profit” which they would explain with youthful logic; “In the interaction between Uganda and India, Ssempa was the Ugandan profit.” These were painful words casually thrown around by some misguided youngsters. They did not reflect the sentiment of the whole Buganda community which accepted me as a son. But in the places where children interacted with minimal adult supervision; the classrooms, playing fields where adults were absent to guide, I was often called painful names, like ‘illegitimate,’ ‘bastard,’ ‘magoba ga Uganda.’ It is a fact of life that some children will mock those who are different or handicapped, maybe they have unusually large ears or nose. This is the foolishness of childhood which fortunately disappears as we grow older. 

Narozali is found in Buyange Parish, Kyanamukakaaka subcounty in Masaka district in the South West of Uganda. It was a large Roman catholic parish with a church, schools and many other projects run by the church. It was located about one hour from Masaka town, on the undulating hills surrounding the shores of Lake Victoria. My mother was a grade one (primary one) teacher at the parish and we stayed in a house provided by the school. My mother was a devout catholic and we attended daily morning mass as well as family evening prayers. We prayed much when there was trouble such as when there was war in the period of 1971-72. In 1971, the president of Uganda, Apollo Milton Obote was overthrown by his star General, Idi Amin Dada in a military takeover that changed Uganda’s political and economic terrain in which I was to grow up. First, the expulsion of Asians in his economic war policy of indigenization was a strange mixture of tragedy and triumph. It was tragic to the Indians whose families had built and run the back bone of the Ugandan economy and were unceremoniously expelled from the country. Most of all the industries, commercial farms, large and small trading shops were owned and run by Indian families who had the technical skills, experience and passion to operate them effectively. They were forced to vacate all of this in a short time not knowing where they were to go. The sudden loss of homes and wealth which had been accumulated for nearly a century led some unfortunate souls to suicides by the river Nile. Others travelled to Canada, England, Kenya and United States where they started a new life. Some ended up succeeding incredibly in their new homes, becoming the economic entrepreneurs of their new homelands. Soon after Idi Amin became president of Uganda, there was an ill-fated attempt to attack and militarily overthrow him by rebels based out of Tanzania. 

Our home of Narozali is in the South West region of Uganda’s territory next to Tanzania and at times, it seemed that we were living in a war zone. Military vehicles, jeeps and noisy Israeli-made warplanes above made it difficult to ignore the ongoing conflict. We spent a lot of time praying to God to intervene and even added special supplications to the Virgin Mary who had a special altar with her monument encased in a specially made grotto. Here we earnestly recited the rosary and asked for divine intervention. Providentially, the war ended soon as the attackers were defeated in a bloody massacre! The early efforts by the coalition of anti-Idi Amini forces to remove him militarily were unsuccessful and suffered huge casualties. For the natives, it was also a mixture of triumph and tragedy. Their struggle for independence from colonial masters had given them political gains without economic gains. The economy was controlled by the Indian merchant families giving little or no space for the emergence of African owned enterprises. This all changed suddenly as Iddi Amin began to apportion out enterprises to the natives. My mother applied to operate a stone quarry but was denied for some reason. However, native Ugandan's got to own and operate all sorts of businesses from industries to merchant shops. While it is true that many ended up being mismanaged and run into the ground, there were others which succeeded. The expulsion of the Asians/ Indians created a leadership vacuum which forced many Ugandans to quickly learn to trade in various enterprises, giving rise to Ugandan owned business. 

As a child of dual Asian-Ugandan ancestry, it was a loss for my father’s people, and a gain for my mother’s people. As Nyinamwiru, the daughter of Bukuku lamented when she learnt that her father had been killed by her son Karabumbi Nduhura who was now the new king, “My ears cause me to hear both evil and good, for is it not my son who has killed Bukuku? My father is dead, but my son reigns, thus I have sorrow on one arm but joy on the other.” This historical account of our ancestors’ dilemma describes my conflicted view of Idi Amin’s expulsion of Indians from Uganda. This view was later to be articulated in my college days by a professor of Political Science at Makerere University who said that Amin’s expulsion of Indians was the single most significant event in economic empowerment of the Ugandan natives. It was quite interesting because, Professor Mahmood Mamdani, was a Ugandan with Asian ancestry, just like me. To date, Uganda, unlike its East African counterparts Kenya and Tanzania has the greatest number of Africans who own business while the other two have businesses still largely owned by the original Asian families who had no Iddi Amin to shake them up. 

Excerpts from "Magoba Ga Uganda" the Auto Biography of Pastor Martin Ssempa..now Coming out later in Dec 2025

A road safety officer stopped us today. My brother was driving, and he presented his valid UAE/Dubai driving licence. The vehicle papers were checked everything was intact. Fire extinguisher? Intact. Warning triangle? Intact. Spare tyre? Intact.

The officer then demanded a Nigerian driver's licence. My brother explained that we don't reside in Nigeria and had only just returned. The officer insisted that a Dubai licence could not be used in Nigeria, even for one day.

I simply asked him to show us the specific law we had violated. Instead of showing the law, the attitude changed. He started saying I was claiming to know everything and that "this is Nigeria."

I also explained that my own Nigerian driver's licence has expired because I no longer drive in Nigeria. I told him I have not driven since I returned and have no intention of renewing a licence for a vehicle I am not driving. He insisted that even if I don't drive, I must renew it.

I asked him: Why should I keep spending money renewing a driver's licence when I have decided not to drive in Nigeria? And why are citizens constantly being suffocated with one charge, renewal or demand after another?

I even asked whether he understood that citizens have constitutional rights and should not be treated as if every interaction with a government officer must end in intimidation or payment. He simply looked at me as though I was the one who had lost my mind.

What made it worse was seeing a condemned truck that clearly should not have been on the road pass right in front of us without being stopped, while we were being held over a valid foreign driver's licence.

When I questioned the double standard, the situation escalated. I made a phone call, and the officer accused me of calling "cultists" to attack them.

The next thing, a JTF team comprising soldiers, police and civil defence arrived aggressively, shouting for everyone to come down from the vehicle. We were three people—my brother, his wife and me. His wife was still inside the vehicle.

They aggressively tried to take my phone when I was recording what was happening. I asked them to first hear our side of the story.

After they eventually listened and confirmed what had happened, we were told to leave and not be aggressive towards officers. But I never came there looking for trouble. I was simply asking questions and trying to document what was happening to us.

They later insisted that I delete the video, which I did in their presence.

Why all this suffocation of citizens?

Why must asking a legitimate question to a government officer suddenly become "insulting an officer," "knowing too much," or "challenging authority"?

Respect for citizens and respect for personnel must work both ways. A uniform is not a licence to intimidate citizens, and citizens should not have to surrender their rights simply because someone in uniform says, "This is Nigeria."

Say NO to citizens' intimidation.

I will never bow to intimidation or oppression.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.
